newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CALL FOR TOUGHER STAND ON S.AFRICAN DRUNK DRIVERS.
newsitem.headline: CALL FOR TOUGHER STAND ON S.AFRICAN DRUNK DRIVERS.

text.p: The South African government was on Friday warned that lowering the allowable blood alcohol content for drivers alone would not reduce the country's high road death toll.

Head of the Medical Research Council's national trauma research programme Johann van der Spuy told the parliamentary transport committee unless this was backed up by tougher law enforcement and an education campaign, it would have no effect.
The new National Road Traffic Bill proposes that the allowable blood alcohol content be reduced from 0.08 to 0.05.
Van der Spuy said a recent survey had found that 47 percent of drivers and 72 percent of pedestrians killed on the roads had blood alcohol levels of 0.08 or higher.
But cutting the blood alcohol rate from 0.15 to 0.08 in 1973 "mattered not an iota on the roads," Van der Spuy said.
"We all want to reduce alcohol on the roads but we are making three mistakes in the process. We think that we can do it by legislation, this is a myth.

"If we just reduce the levels of alcohol and we do not really employ it forcefully on the roads, we are going to repeat the 1973 experience and at the moment we do not really have the infrastructure or the budgets to put it on the road.
He warned that setting blood alcohol levels too low could be counterproductive and he was already hearing people say that "if having had a sherry makes me a criminal, why not have a couple?"
The focus should be on identifying drunk drivers before they had accidents. This should be done through more routine road blocks and checks.
Van der Spuy was particularly concerned about the high number of alcohol-related deaths of pedestrians.

"People do not understand that 45 percent of annual road deaths nationally are pedestrians and in the Cape Peninsula, the problem is much greater. More than two thirds of our road deaths are pedestrians," he said.
Van der Spuy said a way would have to be found to test drivers for drugs which were a further cause of intoxication.
